analysis.one_liner: Requires big campaign spenders to disclose their top donors and closes loopholes on foreign election money.
analysis.headline: All 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 4 independents signed on, but the bill sat in the Rules Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would force corporations, unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups that spend more than $10,000 influencing federal elections to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to name anyone who gave them $10,000 or more. Political ads would have to 'stand by' their messages by listing the group's top five funders on screen. It would also extend the ban on foreign money to digital ads and ballot-measure fights, and make it a crime — punishable by up to five years in prison — to set up a shell company to hide foreign election money.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would finally be able to see who is paying for the political ads they see — including on judicial nominations, where spending is currently not disclosed at all. The bill's own findings note that dark money groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 election cycle with no donor disclosure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting to see who funds campaign ads

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations spending more than $10,000 on campaigns in a two-year cycle would have to report it to the FEC within 24 hours and list every person who gave them $10,000 or more.
Political ads would have to carry an on-screen or audio list of the group's top five funders (top two for radio), extending the 'I approve this message' idea to untraceable outside groups.

The ban on foreign money would be extended to paid web and digital ads and to ballot initiatives and referenda, and it would become a crime punishable by up to five years in prison to form an entity to conceal a foreign national's election contribution.
Spending to support or oppose federal judicial nominations — currently outside campaign finance law entirely — would fall under the same reporting and disclaimer rules.

analysis.who_pays: Organizations that spend money to influence elections — corporations, trade associations, 501(c)(4) 'social welfare' groups, unions, and super PACs — would bear the compliance cost of rapid-fire reporting, and their largest donors would lose anonymity. Large online platforms and ad networks would face new foreign-money and disclaimer rules on political ads.

drawbacks.text: Covered organizations must file within 24 hours of crossing the $10,000 spending threshold and file a certification under penalty of perjury from their top officer, a compliance burden that falls hardest on small or grassroots groups.
The bill acknowledges disclosure can endanger people: it exempts from being named any donor who would face serious threats, harassment, or reprisals.
It only requires disclosure; it does not limit how much money can be spent on elections.

The bill anticipates constitutional challenges: it channels lawsuits against itself into a single fast-track DC federal court and lets any member of Congress intervene, and it includes a severability clause in case parts are struck down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main public benefit — knowing who funds the ads aimed at voters — is large and directly addresses the ~$1 billion in untraceable spending the bill's own findings describe. The costs are real but modest: reporting paperwork for groups that spend on politics, and some legal uncertainty given that top-donor disclosure requirements are the kind of rule that draws First Amendment lawsuits. The bill's biggest weakness is that it does not reduce the money itself, only the secrecy around it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 16, 2023 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration.
The action history shows no further activity: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It had 51 cosponsors — all 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of the 4 independents — with no Republican cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations and donors that spend untraceable money on elections keep the ability to do so: dark money groups, super PAC funders, and any foreign money channeling through shell entities all remain outside the disclosure rules the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DISCLOSE Act and recruited the entire Senate Democratic caucus and three independents to cosponsor it.

for.name: 48 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Every Democratic senator cosponsored the bill.

for.name: 3 of 4 Independent senators
for.what_they_did: Sanders, King, and Sinema cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Amy Klobuchar
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but as committee chair never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the bill stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Republican senators cosponsored or took any recorded step to advance the bill.

against.name: Major business lobbies such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against earlier versions of the DISCLOSE Act, which the House passed in 2010 and 2012 before the measures died in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely on one side of the aisle: all 48 Democrats and 3 of 4 independents cosponsored, while none of the 49 Republicans did.

industries.industry: Dark-money political nonprofits (501(c)(4) groups and trade associations)
industries.note: These groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 cycle without naming donors; the bill would force 24-hour spending reports and top-donor lists. Their interest in anonymity is exactly what voters would have gained the right to see through.

industries.industry: Super PACs and their largest donors
industries.note: Political committees that accept unlimited money would have to report anyone giving $10,000 or more. Donors who currently influence elections anonymously would lose that protection.

industries.industry: Foreign-linked political spenders and shell-entity operators
industries.note: The bill extends the foreign money ban to digital ads and ballot measures and makes it a crime, punishable by up to five years, to build a shell company to hide foreign election money.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and digital ad networks
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more U.S. users would face new foreign-money restrictions and funder-disclaimer requirements on political ads. The rules add compliance friction but also bring paid political ads on these platforms under the same transparency rules voters expect on TV.

Unions are 'covered organizations' under the bill and would face the same 24-hour reporting and top-donor disclosure as corporations. The rules apply to them symmetrically, which is part of the bill's balanced design, but they still bear the compliance cost.
